name: Vera Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small carpentry crew making timber forms and fitting stairs on building sites. My vocational trade certificate opened the door, but I learned the tricky parts by watching an older carpenter correct a bad stair pitch. I use AI now and then to tidy a materials order, then I check every board at the stack. My partner Oren and I have two children in school, a mortgage and less than a month of expenses saved; despite leading the crew, my pay is low for this work. There are only a few other contractors near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a faster materials form is fine if the timber count still gets checked by hand. An order cannot hold up a stair form if the boards are missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My physical work would stay, but our household is already tight. A rain-shortened carpentry week can leave our mortgage waiting for the next pay cheque. A modest software gain does not fix that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the formwork crew and compare any AI order with the timber stack. In the first year I would put twenty from a full pay week into an emergency account if groceries and mortgage are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a rain-shortened week leaving the bank balance low. I want the children to hear us talk about plans, not overdue bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which item goes missing most often?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer boards for stair forms sometimes come in the wrong length. I would count and measure them before the crew cuts the shorter supports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you save twenty every week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, only after a full paid week with the ordinary bills met. I would put nothing away in a rain-shortened week.

say: **Timber counts** still need a person at the stack.
**Faster orders** do little if stair-form boards are missing.
think: My **physical work** stays in the plateau.
A **rain-shortened week** could strain the mortgage with less than a month saved.
do: **Keep** leading formwork and check AI orders against the timber stack.
**Save** twenty from full paid weeks only after food and mortgage clear.
feel: **Anxious** about a rain-shortened week leaving the household short of cash.
S0.quote: A rain-shortened carpentry week can leave our mortgage waiting for the next pay cheque.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** and lower pay coexist with almost no household cushion.
Her **new savings** depend on a full week of wages after essential bills.

steps.text: Keep leading formwork and checking timber orders
Save twenty from full paid weeks after food and mortgage clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and booking will change before robots can put up formwork on a site. I would try a new materials planner only after it gets actual timber lengths right on several jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool cuts ordering staff and a wrong delivery wastes a day, my crew could lose paid hours. We have little saved and few nearby employers, so I could not shrug off repeated short weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the new order planner with five actual formwork jobs and record missing boards and delays. In the first year I would show the manager the log and take a paid Saturday stair repair if a customer books one, putting half the fee away after materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, even while I am willing to test the planner. I cannot pay the mortgage with a screen that says the timber arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the ordered length, delivered length and the hours the crew stood waiting. If the planner gets all five right, I would say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might book Saturday work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A former customer might ask me to fix a loose stair tread at home. I would take it only after giving a price that covers the timber and my time.

say: **Buying and booking** change before physical formwork robots spread.
**Actual timber lengths** should decide whether to use a planner.
think: Wrong **deliveries** could cost my crew paid hours.
Our **thin savings** and few local jobs make repeated short weeks serious.
do: **Test** order planner on five formwork jobs.
**Take** booked Saturday stair repair only at a price covering timber and my time.
**Save** half the earned fee after materials.
feel: **Anxious** about pay despite interest in a proven planner.
S1.quote: I cannot pay the mortgage with a screen that says the timber arrived.
fieldNote: She tests **new planning AI** against lengths and waits, not a sales promise.
Her **side job and savings** require an actual booking, fair price and material costs paid.

steps.text: Learn order planner on five actual formwork jobs
Take booked Saturday stair repair only at a price covering timber and time
Save half of earned stair repair fee after materials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 changes buying and plans, while capable site robots come about 2031. We still have three years of hands-on formwork before those machines can do the whole job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some of our paid formwork shifts to go when robots arrive, even if the first machines stumble on old stairs. With less than a month saved and few nearby contractors, I could not cover a long job search while raising the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for paid practice on a robot formwork setup if the contractor runs a trial, and learn where the stop control is on dead equipment. After 2028 I would apply for a posted local site-checking job only if its wage covers mortgage and food and any required course is paid; until offered, I would keep leading the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and I have woken up thinking about a building site with only half the carpenters on the roster. I would still show up tomorrow and make sure the stair is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test on the robot setup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give it a stair opening that is narrower at the top and see whether it measures both sides. A form built to the average width would not fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no local site-checking post appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep asking nearby contractors about posted work while the current crew still has shifts. I would not pay for a course or move the children on a rumour.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes buying before capable site robots can build formwork around 2031.
think: I expect fewer **paid shifts** after robots arrive.
Our **tiny reserve** and few local employers make a long search frightening.
do: **Learn** robot setup stop controls in paid trial if offered.
**Apply** after 2028 for posted local site-checking only with bill-covering pay and paid course.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected roster cuts and lost sleep.
S2.quote: I have woken up thinking about a building site with only half the carpenters on the roster.
fieldNote: Her **robot practice** is paid learning on actual equipment in a supervised trial, not a course enquiry.
Her **application** requires a posted local job, bill-covering wages and funded training.

steps.text: Learn robot setup stop controls on dead equipment in paid trial if offered
Apply after 2028 for posted local site-checking only with bill-covering pay and paid course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives a contractor time to try robots on awkward stairs before thinking AI reaches buying in 2031. The capable machines arrive around 2034, and I would rather see a failed fitting logged than hidden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be near fifty when a robot could take much of the formwork. I can learn a new site task if someone shows me properly, but a local job with real pay has to exist first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading formwork shifts and ask for a written list of future site roles. If a posted local quality role with a bill-covering wage and paid hands-on training opens, I would take the training before 2031 and apply in the first year after 2031; otherwise I would stay with the crew while jobs remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with five years to make a careful choice. I would not let a quality-course certificate stand in for a building-site pay cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would quality work involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check stair height, the bracing of a timber form and whether the finished edge is safe to walk on. I would want to be on site, not only at a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Oren support retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Oren would want the wage and travel time before agreeing. I think Oren would support it if it covered bills and kept the children in their schools.

say: **Awkward-stair trials** should precede capable site robots that can build formwork around 2034.
**Failed fittings** should stay in the record.
think: I could learn **quality work** if taught on site.
A **local posted job** and bill-covering pay must exist first.
do: **Keep** leading formwork and request a future-role list.
**Take** paid hands-on quality training only for posted local bill-covering vacancy.
**Apply** after 2031 for that posted local role if trained and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test real options.
S3.quote: I would not let a quality-course certificate stand in for a building-site pay cheque.
fieldNote: Her **training plan** is contingent on paid practice and a posted local vacancy.
She links **family stability** to wage, travel time and keeping children in school.

steps.text: Keep formwork shifts while requesting a written role list
Take paid quality training for posted local bill-covering vacancy
Apply after 2031 for posted local quality role if trained and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade puts thinking AI in 2036 and capable building robots around 2039. I would use the time to help my children learn a practical skill and build a reserve from real wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be in my fifties when robots can do the whole site task. Ten years gives us time to save, but I cannot assume a low-paid lead job will fund every year after a machine takes the formwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading sites and move fifty from each full pay cheque into savings after household bills clear. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for posted local site inspection only if the wage covers our bills and any required training is funded; I would stay on formwork until a real offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less pressed than in the fast picture. I want the children to see us build a plan from work, not from a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show them how a square checks a stair corner and how to price timber before promising a repair. They can choose their own trade, but those habits travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the extra fifty is not there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would skip that saving for the week, not take it from the food bill. A full building-site pay cheque can build our cushion only after ordinary costs are covered.

say: **2036 thinking AI** precedes capable building robots around 2039.
**Practical skills** can be taught without promising the same trade forever.
think: Ten years allows **new saving** from full building-site wages if ordinary household bills keep being covered.
Low **lead pay** may still leave future income exposed.
do: **Save** fifty from full pay cheques only after household bills.
**Apply** after 2036 for posted local inspection only with bill-covering pay and funded training.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to improve the reserve.
S4.quote: A full building-site pay cheque can build our cushion only after ordinary costs are covered.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **new saving** from the tiny reserve already held.
Her **later application** retains a posted local job, funded training and a wage covering bills.

steps.text: Keep leading formwork on current building sites
Save fifty from full pay cheques only after household bills
Apply after 2036 for posted local inspection only with bill-covering pay and funded training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because formwork robots around 2031 could cut our paid shifts while the children and mortgage still need income. Paid setup practice and a posted local site-checking job at enough pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks a robot-built stair before a family walks on it. I want the person holding the square to have a name on the sign-off sheet.

portrait: **Vera Lopez**, 43, leads a formwork and stair crew with a vocational trade certificate.
She and partner Oren have **two school-age children**, a mortgage, lower pay and less than a month saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** for orders and tests new planning tools against actual timber lengths.
In **AGI by 2028**, she learns robot stop controls if paid practice is offered and seeks posted local work.
The **2031 and 2036 pictures** let her ask for funded quality work and add new savings from full wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut formwork shifts around 2031 while her family has almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **robot setup practice** would let her learn stop controls before machines reach site work.
A posted local **site-checking job** at bill-covering pay would protect income if shifts fall.
headlineQuote: I want the person holding the square to have a name on the sign-off sheet.
